concepts.def: A cell of the nervous system that carries electrical impulses. It consists of a cell body, containing the cytoplasm and nucleus, with elongated nerve fibres of varying length projecting from it, along which impulses are conducted.
The part of a neuron that contains the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm. The nerve fibres, both the axon and the dendrites, project from it.

A long single nerve fibre projecting from the cell body of a neuron, along which impulses are conducted. In some human motor neurons a single axon extends about a metre from the spinal cord to a muscle.
One of the multiple shorter nerve fibres projecting from the cell body of a neuron. Impulses are conducted along dendrites as well as along the axon.

An elongated projection of a neuron, either an axon or a dendrite, along which electrical impulses are conducted. A nerve fibre is part of a single neuron; a nerve, by contrast, is a bundle of many fibres from many neurons.

A transmembrane protein in the plasma membrane of a neuron that uses energy from ATP to move sodium ions out of the cell and potassium ions into it, against their concentration gradients. Three sodium ions are moved out for every two potassium ions moved in, so the cytoplasm becomes low in sodium ions and high in potassium ions.

The difference in electrical potential (voltage) between the inside and the outside of a cell membrane, conventionally stated as the potential of the inside relative to the outside. It arises because charged ions are unequally distributed across the membrane.

The state of a membrane that has a difference in charge across it, one side being more positive and the other more negative. A resting neuron is polarized because its inside is negatively charged relative to its outside.

The membrane potential of a neuron that is not conducting an impulse, typically about −70 mV (inside negative). It is generated and maintained by the sodium–potassium pump, which establishes concentration gradients, together with the greater leakage of potassium ions out of the cell than of sodium ions into it and the presence of negatively charged proteins inside the cell that cannot cross the membrane.

An action potential that is propagated along a nerve fibre. It is an electrical signal because it involves movement of positively charged ions (sodium and potassium ions) across the membrane, which changes the membrane potential.

A rapid, temporary reversal of the membrane potential of a nerve fibre, in which the inside briefly becomes positive relative to the outside (depolarization) and then returns to the negative resting potential (repolarization). It is propagated along the fibre without decreasing in size.

A very wide non-myelinated axon, up to about 1 mm in diameter, that conducts impulses at about 25 m s⁻¹. This is far faster than narrow non-myelinated fibres, which may be only about 1 µm wide and conduct at around 1 m s⁻¹, showing that conduction speed is positively correlated with axon diameter.

A nerve fibre surrounded by a myelin sheath. Myelinated fibres conduct impulses much faster than non-myelinated fibres of similar diameter; myelinated fibres in mammals can conduct at over 100 m s⁻¹, faster even than a squid giant axon many times wider.

A statistic between −1 and +1 that measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables. The sign shows the direction (positive when the variables rise together, negative when one falls as the other rises) and the magnitude shows the strength, with values near ±1 indicating a strong correlation and values near 0 a weak one. A correlation, however strong, does not by itself show that one variable causes the other.

The square of the correlation coefficient, r², expressed as a value from 0 to 1 or as a percentage. It gives the proportion of the variation in the dependent variable that is explained by variation in the independent variable; for example, if r = 0.9 then R² = 0.81, so 81% of the variation is explained. R² has no sign and so does not indicate the direction of a correlation.

A positive correlation is one in which the dependent variable tends to increase as the independent variable increases, as conduction speed does with axon diameter. A negative correlation is one in which the dependent variable tends to decrease as the independent variable increases, as conduction speed does with animal size.

A junction between a neuron and another cell, either another neuron or an effector cell such as a muscle fibre or gland cell, across which a signal passes by means of a chemical neurotransmitter. A signal can pass across a typical synapse in one direction only.

The presynaptic neuron is the neuron that brings an impulse to a synapse and releases neurotransmitter from its presynaptic membrane. The postsynaptic cell is the neuron or effector cell whose membrane carries the receptors for that neurotransmitter and which is stimulated as a result.

A cell that carries out a response when it is stimulated by a neuron, such as a muscle fibre that contracts or a gland cell that secretes. The synapse between a motor neuron and a muscle fibre is a neuromuscular junction.

A chemical stored in vesicles in the presynaptic neuron and released into the synaptic cleft when an impulse arrives. It diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, passing the signal to the postsynaptic cell.

concepts.term: Calcium as an intracellular signalling chemical
concepts.def: When an action potential depolarizes the presynaptic membrane, calcium channels in that membrane open and calcium ions diffuse into the presynaptic neuron from the surrounding fluid. Inside the neuron the calcium ions act as a signal that causes vesicles of neurotransmitter to fuse with the presynaptic membrane.

The release of neurotransmitter from the presynaptic neuron by fusion of vesicles with the presynaptic membrane, so that their contents are emptied into the synaptic cleft. It is triggered by the entry of calcium ions.
The narrow fluid-filled gap, about 20 nm wide, between the presynaptic membrane and the postsynaptic membrane. Neurotransmitter crosses it by diffusion.

A protein in the postsynaptic membrane to which a neurotransmitter binds. In an excitatory synapse the receptor is, or opens, a channel that lets positively charged ions such as sodium ions diffuse into the postsynaptic cell.

A depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane caused by an excitatory neurotransmitter binding to its receptors and opening channels through which positively charged ions, mainly sodium ions, enter. It brings the membrane potential closer to the threshold for an action potential.

A neurotransmitter used at many types of synapse, including synapses between neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems and neuromuscular junctions between motor neurons and skeletal muscle fibres. Binding of acetylcholine to its receptors on the postsynaptic membrane generates an excitatory postsynaptic potential.

The synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fibre. Acetylcholine released from the motor neuron binds to receptors on the muscle fibre membrane and depolarizes it, leading to contraction.

The membrane potential, typically about −55 mV, that must be reached for voltage-gated sodium channels to open and an action potential to be produced. A depolarization that does not reach threshold fades away without producing an action potential.

A channel protein in the membrane of a nerve fibre that opens when the membrane potential reaches the threshold. Sodium ions then diffuse into the fibre down their concentration gradient, causing depolarization; the channels then close before the membrane repolarizes.

A channel protein in the membrane of a nerve fibre that opens in response to the depolarization of an action potential, slightly later than the sodium channels. Potassium ions diffuse out of the fibre down their concentration gradient, causing repolarization.

The change in membrane potential during an action potential from the negative resting value to a positive value (about +30 mV), caused by the entry of sodium ions through voltage-gated sodium channels.

The return of the membrane potential from its positive peak to the negative resting value, caused by the exit of potassium ions through voltage-gated potassium channels. The sodium–potassium pump does not cause repolarization, but afterwards restores the concentration gradients that the action potential has slightly reduced.

The movement of ions along a nerve fibre, inside and outside it, between a region that is depolarized and the adjacent resting region. Sodium ions that have entered diffuse along the inside of the fibre away from the depolarized region, and outside the fibre sodium ions diffuse towards it, reducing the membrane potential of the adjacent region until it reaches threshold.

The passage of an action potential along a nerve fibre, in which local currents from each depolarized region bring the next region to threshold, opening its voltage-gated sodium channels so that it produces its own action potential. Each region regenerates the action potential in turn, so the impulse does not fade as it travels.

A graph of membrane potential (usually in millivolts) against time (usually in milliseconds), recorded from electrodes placed inside and outside a nerve fibre. A resting potential appears as a steady line at about −70 mV; an action potential appears as a spike that rises to about +30 mV during depolarization, falls during repolarization, may briefly dip below the resting potential, and then returns to it.

The number of action potentials passing along a nerve fibre per second, found from an oscilloscope trace by counting the spikes and dividing by the time in seconds that the trace covers. A stronger stimulus produces a higher frequency of impulses, not larger action potentials.

An insulating layer of membrane, laid down by Schwann cells, that wraps around a myelinated nerve fibre. It is interrupted at intervals by nodes of Ranvier and prevents ion movement across the parts of the membrane it covers.
A short gap in the myelin sheath of a myelinated fibre where the membrane is exposed. Ion pumps and voltage-gated channels are clustered at the nodes, so action potentials occur only there.

Propagation of an action potential along a myelinated fibre from one node of Ranvier to the next. Local currents spread rapidly along the insulated section between nodes and depolarize the next node to threshold, so the action potential appears to jump from node to node. Because only the nodes have to be depolarized, conduction is much faster than in a non-myelinated fibre.

A type of pesticide that binds to acetylcholine receptors at synapses in the central nervous system of insects. The receptors can then no longer respond normally to acetylcholine, so synaptic transmission is blocked and the insect is paralysed and dies.

A drug that blocks reuptake of the neurotransmitter dopamine by binding to the transporter proteins that would return dopamine to the presynaptic neuron. Dopamine therefore remains in the synaptic cleft and continues to stimulate the postsynaptic neuron.

The removal of neurotransmitter from the synaptic cleft by transporter proteins that move it back into the presynaptic neuron, ending its action on the postsynaptic receptors. Blocking reuptake prolongs and intensifies the stimulation of the postsynaptic cell.

A neurotransmitter, such as GABA, whose binding to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane opens channels that make the inside of the postsynaptic cell more negative, for example by letting chloride ions in or potassium ions out. This hyperpolarizes the membrane and makes an action potential less likely.
A change in membrane potential to a value more negative than the resting potential, for example from −70 mV to −75 mV. A hyperpolarized membrane is further from the threshold potential.

A hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane caused by an inhibitory neurotransmitter, which moves the membrane potential further from threshold and so reduces the likelihood that the postsynaptic neuron will produce an action potential.

The adding together of the postsynaptic potentials produced by several presynaptic neurons acting on one postsynaptic neuron. Excitatory potentials depolarize and inhibitory potentials hyperpolarize, so the combined effect is their net sum; an action potential is produced only if this net change reaches threshold.

The principle that a postsynaptic neuron either produces a full-sized action potential, if the summed postsynaptic potentials reach threshold, or produces none at all. Postsynaptic potentials themselves are graded in size, but the action potential they may trigger is not.

The unspecialized ending of a sensory neuron in the skin that responds to painful stimuli. Its membrane has channels for positively charged ions that open in response to high temperature, acid, or certain chemicals such as capsaicin. Entry of positively charged ions depolarizes the membrane to threshold, and impulses then pass along the neuron to the brain.

The chemical in chilli peppers that produces a burning sensation. It opens channels for positively charged ions in free nerve endings, the same response these endings give to high temperature, so the brain perceives pain even though the tissue is not hot.

The awareness of pain, which occurs in the brain when impulses from free nerve endings reach it. The nerve endings in the skin detect the stimulus and generate the impulses, but the pain itself is perceived in the brain, not in the skin.

A property of a whole system that arises from the interaction of its components and is not a property of any component on its own. Consciousness is an emergent property of the brain: it arises from the interaction of very many neurons, and no individual neuron is conscious.

The state of awareness of oneself and one's surroundings. It emerges from the interaction of the individual neurons of the brain and cannot be located in, or explained by, any single neuron or its signals.

mcqs.q: A motor neuron has its cell body in the spinal cord and a single fibre about 1 m long that reaches a muscle in the foot. What is this fibre?
options: One of the neuron's several axons, each of which reaches a different muscle in the leg.
An axon: a single long fibre along which impulses are conducted away from the cell body.
A nerve, because a fibre this long must be made of many neurons joined end to end.
A connecting fibre that links the neuron to the muscle but is not part of the neuron itself.
mcqs.specStatementText: A neuron is one cell with a body and long fibres
mcqs.explain: An axon is a long single fibre projecting from the cell body. A motor neuron's axon can extend about a metre from the spinal cord to a muscle, and impulses are conducted along it.
rationales: A student who thinks a neuron has several axons picks this. In fact a neuron has a single axon; its branches near the end are terminals of that one axon.
An axon is a long single fibre projecting from the cell body. A motor neuron's axon can extend about a metre from the spinal cord to a muscle, and impulses are conducted along it.
A student who confuses a nerve with a neuron picks this. In fact one neuron's axon can be a metre long; a nerve is a bundle of many such fibres.
A student who sees fibres as separate wiring picks this. In fact the fibre is part of the neuron: an extension of its cytoplasm surrounded by its own membrane.

mcqs.q: How does the sodium–potassium pump contribute to the resting potential of a neuron?
options: It uses energy from ATP to move potassium ions out of the neuron and sodium ions in across the membrane, building up concentration gradients of both ions.
It lets sodium and potassium ions diffuse down their concentration gradients through its channel, without using any ATP at all.
It uses energy from ATP to move sodium ions out of the neuron and potassium ions in, building up concentration gradients of both ions.
It is switched off while the neuron is at rest, so that no ATP is used until an impulse arrives at the membrane of the neuron.
mcqs.specStatementText: Pumping ions sets up the resting potential
mcqs.explain: Energy from ATP drives the pumping of sodium and potassium ions in opposite directions across the membrane: sodium ions out and potassium ions in. The gradients this establishes, together with unequal leakage of the two ions, generate the negative resting potential.
rationales: A student who has the two ions the wrong way round picks this. In fact sodium ions are pumped out and potassium ions in, so the cytoplasm is high in potassium ions and low in sodium ions.
A student who confuses a pump with a channel picks this. In fact the pump moves ions against their gradients, which requires energy from ATP; diffusion cannot build a gradient.

Energy from ATP drives the pumping of sodium and potassium ions in opposite directions across the membrane: sodium ions out and potassium ions in. The gradients this establishes, together with unequal leakage of the two ions, generate the negative resting potential.
A student who thinks 'resting' means inactive picks this. In fact the pump works continuously at rest, and it is this pumping that maintains the resting potential.

mcqs.q: Measurements on a resting neuron show that potassium ions are about 30 times more concentrated inside than outside and sodium ions about 10 times more concentrated outside than inside, yet the inside is at −70 mV relative to the outside. Which explanation of the negative resting potential is consistent with these measurements?
options: All the positively charged ions are pumped out of the cytoplasm by the sodium–potassium pump, leaving only negatively charged ions inside the neuron.
Positive ions diffuse out through the pump faster than they diffuse in, because the pump is simply a channel that favours movement outwards.
The membrane is completely impermeable at rest, so the charge left over from the last impulse cannot leak away across it.
The pump moves three sodium ions out for every two potassium ions in, and potassium ions leak back out faster than sodium ions leak in.
mcqs.specStatementText: Pumping ions sets up the resting potential
mcqs.explain: Each cycle of the pump removes more positive charge than it brings in, and the membrane is much more permeable to potassium ions than to sodium ions, so more positive charge leaks out than in. Negatively charged proteins that cannot leave the cytoplasm add to the effect, so the inside is about −70 mV relative to the outside.
rationales: A student who reads 'inside negative' as meaning no positive ions inside picks this. In fact the cytoplasm is rich in potassium ions; the negative potential comes from a small imbalance, not the absence of positive ions.
A student who thinks the pump is a channel picks this. In fact the pump uses ATP to move ions against their gradients; it is not a channel and ions do not diffuse through it.
A student who thinks nothing happens at rest picks this. In fact ions leak across the resting membrane continuously and the pump works continuously to maintain the gradients.

Each cycle of the pump removes more positive charge than it brings in, and the membrane is much more permeable to potassium ions than to sodium ions, so more positive charge leaks out than in. Negatively charged proteins that cannot leave the cytoplasm add to the effect, so the inside is about −70 mV relative to the outside.

mcqs.q: A neuron is treated with a chemical that stops it producing ATP. Which prediction about its resting potential is correct?
options: It gradually falls towards zero, because the pump stops and the ion gradients run down as ions leak across the membrane.
It stays the same, because a neuron at rest is inactive and does not need to use ATP for anything until an impulse arrives.
It stays the same, because the pump moves ions passively down their gradients and does not need ATP in order to work.
It becomes more positive straight away, because the pump can no longer remove the positive ions that had all been kept outside.
mcqs.specStatementText: Pumping ions sets up the resting potential
mcqs.explain: The resting potential depends on gradients that are maintained by pumping driven by ATP. Without ATP the pump stops, leakage of ions continues, and the gradients and the potential they generate decay gradually.
rationales: The resting potential depends on gradients that are maintained by pumping driven by ATP. Without ATP the pump stops, leakage of ions continues, and the gradients and the potential they generate decay gradually.
A student who thinks a resting neuron uses no energy picks this. In fact maintaining the resting potential is an active process that consumes ATP continuously.
A student who confuses the pump with a channel picks this. In fact the pump moves ions against their gradients and cannot work without energy from ATP.

A student who thinks the resting potential comes from all positive ions being outside picks this. In fact the cytoplasm is rich in potassium ions; the gradients run down gradually by leakage, so the potential decays slowly towards zero rather than jumping positive.

mcqs.q: Why is a nerve impulse described as an electrical signal?
options: It consists of electrons flowing along the inside of the fibre, in the same way as a current in a metal wire.
It consists of positively charged ions moving across the membrane, which changes the membrane potential.
It consists of neurotransmitter molecules travelling along the fibre and carrying their electrical charge with them.
It consists of sodium ions flowing along the whole length of the fibre from one end of it to the other.
mcqs.specStatementText: A nerve impulse is a travelling reversal of membrane potential
mcqs.explain: A nerve impulse is electrical because it involves movement of positively charged ions, sodium and potassium ions, across the membrane of the nerve fibre, reversing and then restoring the membrane potential.
rationales: A student who applies the wiring analogy literally picks this. In fact no electrons flow along the axon; the charge carriers are ions crossing the membrane.

A nerve impulse is electrical because it involves movement of positively charged ions, sodium and potassium ions, across the membrane of the nerve fibre, reversing and then restoring the membrane potential.
A student who generalizes the chemical signal at synapses to the whole neuron picks this. In fact neurotransmitters act only at synapses; along the fibre the signal is a change in membrane potential.

A student who thinks the ions themselves travel the length of the axon picks this. In fact ions cross the membrane at each point in turn; the impulse travels but the individual ions move only a short distance.

mcqs.q: Electrodes inside and outside an axon show that the inside briefly becomes positive relative to the outside as an impulse passes. What causes this change?
options: Potassium ions move into the axon across the membrane at that point.
Electrons move out of the axon along the inner surface of its membrane.
Sodium ions move into the axon across the membrane at that point.
Sodium ions arriving from further back along the axon accumulate at that point.
mcqs.specStatementText: A nerve impulse is a travelling reversal of membrane potential
mcqs.explain: During an action potential sodium ions diffuse into the axon through the membrane, adding positive charge inside so that the membrane potential briefly reverses to positive. The impulse is electrical because of this movement of positively charged ions.
rationales: A student who has the ion directions swapped picks this. In fact potassium ions move out of the axon, and they do so later, restoring the negative inside.
A student who thinks of the impulse as electron flow picks this. In fact there is no flow of electrons; positive ions entering the axon make the inside positive.

During an action potential sodium ions diffuse into the axon through the membrane, adding positive charge inside so that the membrane potential briefly reverses to positive. The impulse is electrical because of this movement of positively charged ions.

A student who thinks ions travel along the axon picks this. In fact the sodium ions that make this point positive enter through the membrane at this point; they do not travel along the axon from behind.

mcqs.q: Conduction speeds were measured in three nerve fibres. Fibre P (a squid giant axon) is non-myelinated, 500 µm in diameter, and conducts at 25 m s⁻¹. Fibre Q is non-myelinated, 1 µm in diameter, and conducts at 1 m s⁻¹. Fibre R is myelinated, 10 µm in diameter, and conducts at 60 m s⁻¹. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
options: Myelin speeds up fibre R because the myelin sheath itself conducts the electrical current along the length of the fibre.
Diameter has no effect on speed, so the difference between P and Q must be caused by the type of animal they came from.
Fibre R must come from a larger animal than fibre P, because larger animals conduct nerve impulses faster.
Speed rises with diameter in non-myelinated fibres, and myelination lets a narrow fibre conduct faster than a much wider one.
mcqs.specStatementText: Wider and myelinated fibres conduct faster
mcqs.explain: P and Q are both non-myelinated and the wider one is far faster, showing the positive correlation between diameter and speed. R is fifty times narrower than P yet faster, showing that myelination increases speed more than a large diameter does.
rationales: A student who thinks myelin is a conductor picks this. In fact myelin is an insulator; it speeds conduction by restricting action potentials to the nodes, and the data say nothing about myelin conducting.
A student who thinks only myelination matters picks this. In fact P and Q differ only in diameter and their speeds differ 25-fold, which is direct evidence that diameter affects speed.
A student who assumes speed scales with body size picks this. In fact conduction speed is negatively correlated with animal size, and the data give no information about the animals' sizes.

P and Q are both non-myelinated and the wider one is far faster, showing the positive correlation between diameter and speed. R is fifty times narrower than P yet faster, showing that myelination increases speed more than a large diameter does.

mcqs.q: In a study of axon diameter and conduction speed, the correlation coefficient was r = +0.90. Which statement about the coefficient of determination is correct?
options: R² = 0.81, so about 81% of the variation in speed is explained by variation in diameter.
R² = 0.90, so about 90% of the variation in speed is explained by the variation in diameter.
R² = 0.81, so about 81% of the fibres measured conducted faster when they had a larger diameter.
R² = 0.81, which proves that a larger diameter is the cause of the faster conduction speed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Wider and myelinated fibres conduct faster
mcqs.explain: The coefficient of determination is the square of the correlation coefficient: 0.90² = 0.81. It evaluates the degree to which variation in the independent variable (diameter) explains the variation in the dependent variable (speed), here 81%.
rationales: The coefficient of determination is the square of the correlation coefficient: 0.90² = 0.81. It evaluates the degree to which variation in the independent variable (diameter) explains the variation in the dependent variable (speed), here 81%.
A student who uses r itself as the proportion explained picks this. In fact R² is r squared, 0.81, so 81% of the variation is explained.
A student who reads R² as a fraction of data points picks this. In fact R² describes how much of the variation in speed is accounted for by diameter, not how many fibres follow the trend.
A student who treats a strong correlation as proof of cause picks this. In fact R² measures the strength of the statistical association; causation would need experimental evidence or a mechanism.

mcqs.q: Across a range of animal species, the correlation coefficient between body size and nerve impulse conduction speed was r = −0.85. What does this value show?
options: A weak correlation, because a negative coefficient shows a smaller effect than a positive one would.
A strong negative correlation: speed tends to fall as body size rises, and R² is about 0.72.
That an increase in body size is the direct cause of slower impulses in the larger species.
That about 85% of the variation in conduction speed is explained by the variation in body size.
mcqs.specStatementText: Wider and myelinated fibres conduct faster
mcqs.explain: The sign of r shows the direction (negative: speed falls as size rises) and the magnitude shows the strength (0.85 is close to 1, so strong). The coefficient of determination is (−0.85)² = 0.7225, so about 72% of the variation in speed is explained by body size.
rationales: A student who reads the minus sign as meaning 'weak' picks this. In fact the sign gives the direction only; a magnitude of 0.85 is a strong correlation whichever sign it carries.

The sign of r shows the direction (negative: speed falls as size rises) and the magnitude shows the strength (0.85 is close to 1, so strong). The coefficient of determination is (−0.85)² = 0.7225, so about 72% of the variation in speed is explained by body size.
A student who treats correlation as causation picks this. In fact a correlation coefficient measures association; it cannot show that body size causes the difference in speed.
A student who uses r as the proportion explained picks this. In fact that proportion is R² = 0.85² = 0.72, so about 72%.

mcqs.q: Which statement about a synapse is correct?
options: A signal can pass across it in either direction, depending on which of the two neurons is stimulated first.
It is found only where two neurons meet, so muscle fibres are stimulated directly by the nerve impulse.
A signal can pass across it in one direction only, from the presynaptic cell to the postsynaptic cell.
The action potential jumps across the gap as an electrical spark, so no chemical is needed to cross the cleft.
mcqs.specStatementText: Synapses join neurons to neurons or to effectors, one way only
mcqs.explain: A signal can only pass in one direction across a typical synapse, because neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic membrane and its receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane.
rationales: A student who pictures the synapse as a simple gap picks this. In fact only one side releases neurotransmitter and only the other has receptors, so transmission is one-way.
A student who has only seen neuron-to-neuron synapses picks this. In fact synapses also occur between neurons and effector cells; a neuromuscular junction is a synapse.
A signal can only pass in one direction across a typical synapse, because neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic membrane and its receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane.
A student who assumes electricity bridges the cleft picks this. In fact the signal crosses the cleft as a neurotransmitter that diffuses to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

mcqs.q: Why can a signal pass in only one direction across a synapse?
options: Electric current can only cross the cleft from the more positive presynaptic membrane to the more negative postsynaptic one.
Calcium ions can only diffuse across the cleft from the presynaptic side, because that is where they are concentrated.
Carrier proteins in the cleft actively transport the neurotransmitter towards the postsynaptic membrane only.
Only the presynaptic neuron stores neurotransmitter in vesicles, and only the postsynaptic membrane has receptors for it.
mcqs.specStatementText: Synapses join neurons to neurons or to effectors, one way only
mcqs.explain: The two sides of a synapse are structurally different. Neurotransmitter can be released only from the presynaptic membrane, and it can act only where there are receptors, which are on the postsynaptic membrane, so the signal is one-way.
rationales: A student who thinks the impulse crosses the cleft electrically picks this. In fact no current crosses the cleft; a chemical neurotransmitter carries the signal.
A student who thinks calcium is the messenger across the cleft picks this. In fact calcium ions enter the presynaptic neuron and act inside it; they do not cross the cleft.
A student who thinks neurotransmitter is pumped across the cleft picks this. In fact it diffuses through the fluid in the cleft; there are no carrier proteins in the cleft itself.

The two sides of a synapse are structurally different. Neurotransmitter can be released only from the presynaptic membrane, and it can act only where there are receptors, which are on the postsynaptic membrane, so the signal is one-way.

mcqs.q: What is the role of calcium ions in the release of neurotransmitter from a presynaptic neuron?
options: Depolarization of the presynaptic membrane opens calcium channels; calcium ions enter and signal vesicles to fuse with the membrane.
Calcium ions are released from the presynaptic neuron and diffuse across the cleft, where they then depolarize the postsynaptic membrane.
Calcium ions have no role, because neurotransmitter simply diffuses out through the presynaptic membrane when an impulse arrives.
Calcium ions provide the energy for carrier proteins to pump the neurotransmitter across the synaptic cleft to its postsynaptic receptors.
mcqs.specStatementText: Calcium entry triggers neurotransmitter release
mcqs.explain: When an action potential depolarizes the presynaptic membrane, calcium ions are taken up into the neuron. Inside the neuron they act as a signalling chemical that causes vesicles of neurotransmitter to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing it into the cleft.
rationales: When an action potential depolarizes the presynaptic membrane, calcium ions are taken up into the neuron. Inside the neuron they act as a signalling chemical that causes vesicles of neurotransmitter to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing it into the cleft.
A student who confuses calcium with the neurotransmitter picks this. In fact calcium ions move into the presynaptic neuron and act inside it; the neurotransmitter is what crosses the cleft.
A student who assumes release is passive diffusion picks this. In fact neurotransmitter is stored in vesicles and released by exocytosis, which is triggered by calcium ion entry.
A student who thinks neurotransmitter is actively transported across the cleft picks this. In fact it diffuses across the cleft; calcium ions are a signal for release, not an energy source.

mcqs.q: Calcium ions were removed from the fluid around a synapse. When the presynaptic neuron was stimulated, action potentials still reached the presynaptic terminal, but no response was recorded in the postsynaptic neuron. What does this result show?
options: Calcium ions are the chemical that normally crosses the cleft and stimulates the postsynaptic neuron to respond.
Entry of calcium ions is needed for neurotransmitter to be released, but not for the impulse to reach the terminal.
The neurotransmitter should have diffused out regardless, so the postsynaptic receptors must have been damaged.
Calcium ions are needed to power the active transport of neurotransmitter across the cleft to the postsynaptic membrane.
mcqs.specStatementText: Calcium entry triggers neurotransmitter release
mcqs.explain: The action potential arrived normally, so calcium is not needed for conduction along the axon. Transmission failed at the synapse, which is explained by calcium ions being required to enter the terminal and signal the vesicles to release neurotransmitter.
rationales: A student who thinks calcium is the messenger across the cleft picks this. In fact the result is explained by calcium acting inside the presynaptic neuron to trigger release of the neurotransmitter, which is what crosses the cleft.

The action potential arrived normally, so calcium is not needed for conduction along the axon. Transmission failed at the synapse, which is explained by calcium ions being required to enter the terminal and signal the vesicles to release neurotransmitter.

A student who thinks release is passive diffusion cannot explain the result and blames the receptors. In fact release requires calcium ion entry, so removing calcium prevents release; nothing else need have changed.
A student who thinks neurotransmitter is pumped across the cleft picks this. In fact neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft; calcium ions are the signal for its release from vesicles.

mcqs.q: How does acetylcholine generate an excitatory postsynaptic potential?
options: It diffuses across the cleft and enters the postsynaptic cell, where it depolarizes the membrane from the inside.
It is actively transported across the cleft by carrier proteins, which use ATP to push it into the postsynaptic cell.
It diffuses across the cleft and binds to transmembrane receptors, opening channels through which sodium ions enter the postsynaptic cell.
It diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors, opening channels through which potassium ions enter the postsynaptic cell.
mcqs.specStatementText: Neurotransmitter opens channels and depolarizes the postsynaptic cell
mcqs.explain: Acetylcholine diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to transmembrane receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. Binding opens channels for positively charged ions, mainly sodium ions, which enter and depolarize the membrane, producing an excitatory postsynaptic potential.
rationales: A student who thinks the neurotransmitter goes into the next cell picks this. In fact acetylcholine binds to receptors on the outer surface of the postsynaptic membrane and stays outside; ions entering through the opened channels cause the depolarization.

A student who thinks crossing the cleft needs active transport picks this. In fact acetylcholine diffuses across the narrow cleft and binds to receptors; it is not pumped and it does not enter the cell.

Acetylcholine diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to transmembrane receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. Binding opens channels for positively charged ions, mainly sodium ions, which enter and depolarize the membrane, producing an excitatory postsynaptic potential.

A student who has the ions swapped picks this. In fact the channels opened by acetylcholine at an excitatory synapse let sodium ions enter; potassium ions are more concentrated inside and would not enter.

mcqs.q: A motor neuron forms a neuromuscular junction with a skeletal muscle fibre. Which statement about acetylcholine at this junction is correct?
options: It is found only at neuromuscular junctions, because synapses between two neurons use different neurotransmitters.
It cannot be involved here, because synapses form only between two neurons and the muscle fibre is stimulated electrically.
It passes through the membrane into the muscle fibre and triggers contraction directly from inside the cell.
It is the same neurotransmitter used at many synapses between neurons, and here it binds to receptors on the muscle fibre membrane.
mcqs.specStatementText: Neurotransmitter opens channels and depolarizes the postsynaptic cell
mcqs.explain: Acetylcholine exists in many types of synapse, including synapses between neurons and neuromuscular junctions. At the neuromuscular junction it binds to transmembrane receptors on the muscle fibre, depolarizing it and generating an excitatory postsynaptic potential.
rationales: A student who has met acetylcholine only at the neuromuscular junction picks this. In fact acetylcholine is used at many types of synapse, including many between neurons.
A student who does not classify the neuromuscular junction as a synapse picks this. In fact it is a synapse between a neuron and an effector cell, and acetylcholine is its neurotransmitter.
A student who thinks the neurotransmitter enters the postsynaptic cell picks this. In fact acetylcholine binds to receptors on the outside of the muscle fibre membrane and does not enter it.

Acetylcholine exists in many types of synapse, including synapses between neurons and neuromuscular junctions. At the neuromuscular junction it binds to transmembrane receptors on the muscle fibre, depolarizing it and generating an excitatory postsynaptic potential.

mcqs.q: Which sequence of events produces depolarization and then repolarization during an action potential?
options: Voltage-gated sodium channels open at threshold and sodium ions enter; these channels then close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, so potassium ions leave.
Voltage-gated potassium channels open at threshold and potassium ions enter; these then close and voltage-gated sodium channels open, so sodium ions leave.
Voltage-gated sodium channels open at threshold and sodium ions enter; the sodium–potassium pump then actively pumps the sodium ions back out to repolarize the membrane.
Sodium channels open in proportion to the stimulus, with no threshold, and the size of the action potential then matches the strength of the stimulus applied.
mcqs.specStatementText: Voltage-gated channels drive depolarization and repolarization
mcqs.explain: When the threshold potential is reached, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions diffuse in, depolarizing the membrane to about +30 mV. The sodium channels then close and voltage-gated potassium channels open; potassium ions diffuse out and the membrane repolarizes.
rationales: When the threshold potential is reached, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions diffuse in, depolarizing the membrane to about +30 mV. The sodium channels then close and voltage-gated potassium channels open; potassium ions diffuse out and the membrane repolarizes.

A student who has the two ions swapped picks this. In fact sodium ions enter to depolarize the membrane and potassium ions leave to repolarize it; the concentration gradients make the reverse impossible.

A student who assigns repolarization to the pump picks this. In fact repolarization is caused by potassium ions leaving through voltage-gated channels; the pump is far too slow and only restores the gradients afterwards.
A student who forgets the threshold picks this. In fact voltage-gated sodium channels open only when threshold is reached, and the action potential is then always the same size.

mcqs.q: The resting potential of a neuron is −70 mV and its threshold potential is −55 mV. A weak stimulus depolarizes the membrane to −60 mV. What happens next?
options: A small action potential is produced, in proportion to the size of the stimulus that was applied to the membrane.
The membrane returns to rest: threshold was not reached, so voltage-gated sodium channels stay closed.
The membrane has become hyperpolarized, so no action potential can be produced until it recovers to −70 mV.
A full action potential is produced, because the voltage-gated channels holding the membrane at −70 mV have been disturbed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Voltage-gated channels drive depolarization and repolarization
mcqs.explain: −60 mV is less depolarized than the threshold of −55 mV. Voltage-gated sodium channels open only when the threshold potential is reached, so no action potential is produced and the small depolarization fades back to −70 mV.
rationales: A student who thinks action potentials are graded picks this. In fact there are no small action potentials: below threshold nothing happens, and at threshold a full-sized one occurs.

−60 mV is less depolarized than the threshold of −55 mV. Voltage-gated sodium channels open only when the threshold potential is reached, so no action potential is produced and the small depolarization fades back to −70 mV.

A student who thinks depolarization means becoming more negative reads −60 mV as hyperpolarization. In fact −60 mV is less negative than −70 mV, so this is a small depolarization, just not enough to reach threshold.

A student who thinks voltage-gated channels maintain the resting potential picks this. In fact those channels are closed at rest and open only at threshold; a depolarization to −60 mV does not reach −55 mV, so they stay shut and the membrane returns to rest.

mcqs.q: A drug blocks the voltage-gated potassium channels in an axon. Which effect on its action potentials is predicted?
options: Repolarization is unaffected, because the sodium–potassium pump returns the membrane potential to its resting value.
Depolarization cannot occur, because potassium ions can no longer enter the axon to make the inside positive.
Depolarization occurs normally, but repolarization is much slower, so each action potential lasts longer.
The resting potential cannot be maintained, so the axon can no longer produce any action potentials at all.
mcqs.specStatementText: Voltage-gated channels drive depolarization and repolarization
mcqs.explain: Depolarization depends on voltage-gated sodium channels, which are unaffected. Repolarization depends on potassium ions leaving through voltage-gated potassium channels; with these blocked, the return to the resting potential relies on slower leakage, so the action potential is prolonged.
rationales: A student who thinks the pump repolarizes the membrane picks this. In fact repolarization is the rapid exit of potassium ions through voltage-gated channels, so blocking them slows repolarization markedly.
A student who has the ions swapped picks this. In fact depolarization is caused by sodium ions entering, so blocking potassium channels does not prevent it.

Depolarization depends on voltage-gated sodium channels, which are unaffected. Repolarization depends on potassium ions leaving through voltage-gated potassium channels; with these blocked, the return to the resting potential relies on slower leakage, so the action potential is prolonged.

A student who thinks voltage-gated channels maintain the resting potential picks this. In fact these channels are closed at rest; the resting potential depends on the pump and leak channels, so it is maintained and action potentials can still begin.

mcqs.q: How do local currents propagate an action potential along an axon?
options: Sodium ions that entered at the start travel along the whole axon to its end, carrying the depolarization with them.
Sodium ions that entered diffuse to the next region and depolarize it fully, so no voltage-gated channels are needed there.
Electrons released when the sodium channels open flow along the inside of the axon, depolarizing the whole length at once.
Sodium ions that entered diffuse along the inside of the axon to the next region, bringing it to threshold so its sodium channels open.
mcqs.specStatementText: Local currents carry the action potential along
mcqs.explain: Sodium ions entering at the depolarized region diffuse along the inside of the axon to the adjacent region, while outside the axon sodium ions diffuse towards the depolarized region. These local currents reduce the membrane potential of the adjacent region until threshold is reached and its voltage-gated sodium channels open, regenerating the action potential.
rationales: A student who thinks the same ions travel the length of the axon picks this. In fact each region admits its own sodium ions once it reaches threshold; the ions that entered move only to the neighbouring region.

A student who thinks the local current carries the whole depolarization picks this. In fact local currents only bring the next region to threshold; its own voltage-gated sodium channels then produce the full depolarization.
A student who thinks the impulse is electron flow picks this. In fact local currents are movements of ions, and the action potential is regenerated region by region, not all at once.

Sodium ions entering at the depolarized region diffuse along the inside of the axon to the adjacent region, while outside the axon sodium ions diffuse towards the depolarized region. These local currents reduce the membrane potential of the adjacent region until threshold is reached and its voltage-gated sodium channels open, regenerating the action potential.

mcqs.q: An axon is cooled so that diffusion of ions becomes slower. Which prediction about conduction of impulses along it is correct?
options: Conduction is slower, because local currents take longer to bring each adjacent region of membrane to threshold.
Conduction is slower, because the sodium ions take longer to travel from one end of the axon to the other.
Conduction is unchanged, because the impulse is carried by electrons, whose movement is not affected by temperature.
Conduction is unchanged, because each region is depolarized directly by the one before it without any diffusion of ions.
mcqs.specStatementText: Local currents carry the action potential along
mcqs.explain: Propagation depends on diffusion of sodium ions inside and outside the axon to reduce the membrane potential of the next region to threshold. Slower diffusion means each region reaches threshold later, so the action potential travels more slowly.
rationales: Propagation depends on diffusion of sodium ions inside and outside the axon to reduce the membrane potential of the next region to threshold. Slower diffusion means each region reaches threshold later, so the action potential travels more slowly.

A student who thinks the ions travel the whole length picks this. In fact sodium ions diffuse only to the adjacent region; the delay is in bringing each region to threshold, not in a long journey by the ions.
A student who thinks of the axon as a wire picks this. In fact the impulse depends on diffusion of ions, which is slowed by cooling.
A student who thinks the depolarization is simply handed on picks this. In fact the link between regions is diffusion of sodium ions, the local current, so slowing diffusion slows conduction.

mcqs.q: An oscilloscope trace of an axon shows a steady −70 mV, then a rapid rise to +30 mV at 1 ms, a fall back through −70 mV by 3 ms, a brief dip to −80 mV, and a return to −70 mV. What is happening between 1 ms and 3 ms?
options: Repolarization: voltage-gated potassium channels are open and potassium ions are entering the axon.
Repolarization: voltage-gated potassium channels are open and potassium ions are leaving the axon.
Repolarization: the sodium–potassium pump is actively moving sodium ions back out of the axon.
Depolarization: the membrane potential is becoming more negative as the polarity is being removed from it.
mcqs.specStatementText: Reading an oscilloscope trace
mcqs.explain: The fall from the +30 mV peak back to the resting potential is repolarization. It is caused by voltage-gated potassium channels opening after the sodium channels close, so that potassium ions diffuse out and the inside becomes negative again. The dip to −80 mV is a brief hyperpolarization: the voltage-gated potassium channels are slow to close, so potassium ions continue to leave for a moment after the resting potential is reached, and the membrane returns to −70 mV once they have closed.
rationales: A student who has the direction of potassium movement wrong picks this. In fact potassium ions leave the axon, removing positive charge and so making the inside negative again.

The fall from the +30 mV peak back to the resting potential is repolarization. It is caused by voltage-gated potassium channels opening after the sodium channels close, so that potassium ions diffuse out and the inside becomes negative again. The dip to −80 mV is a brief hyperpolarization: the voltage-gated potassium channels are slow to close, so potassium ions continue to leave for a moment after the resting potential is reached, and the membrane returns to −70 mV once they have closed.

A student who credits the pump with repolarization picks this. In fact a fall of 100 mV in 2 ms is produced by potassium ions diffusing out through voltage-gated channels; the pump restores gradients much more slowly afterwards.
A student who thinks depolarization means becoming more negative picks this. In fact depolarization is the rise to +30 mV before 1 ms; the return to negative values is repolarization.

mcqs.q: An oscilloscope trace covering 60 ms shows 15 action potentials. What is the frequency of impulses?
options: 0.25 impulses per second
4 impulses per second
250 impulses per second
15 impulses per second
mcqs.specStatementText: Reading an oscilloscope trace
mcqs.explain: 60 ms is 0.060 s, so the frequency is 15 ÷ 0.060 = 250 impulses per second. The number of impulses per second is measured from a trace by counting the spikes and dividing by the time covered, in seconds.
rationales: A student who divides by 60 without converting milliseconds to seconds picks this. In fact 60 ms is 0.060 s, so the answer is a thousand times larger: 250.
A student who divides the time by the number of spikes picks this. In fact 60 ÷ 15 = 4 ms is the interval between impulses; frequency is spikes divided by time in seconds.

60 ms is 0.060 s, so the frequency is 15 ÷ 0.060 = 250 impulses per second. The number of impulses per second is measured from a trace by counting the spikes and dividing by the time covered, in seconds.
A student who takes the number of spikes as the frequency picks this. In fact 15 spikes were recorded in only 60 ms, so in a full second there would be 250.

mcqs.q: Two oscilloscope traces were recorded from the same sensory neuron. With a weak stimulus there were 5 action potentials in 100 ms; with a strong stimulus there were 20 action potentials in 100 ms. In both traces every action potential peaked at +30 mV. What do the traces show?
options: The recording must be faulty, because a stronger stimulus should produce action potentials with a higher peak.
The stronger stimulus made each impulse travel faster, so more of them reached the electrode in the time available.
The neuron fired 5 impulses per second with the weak stimulus and 20 impulses per second with the strong stimulus.
Stimulus strength is coded by the frequency of impulses, while the size of each action potential stays fixed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Reading an oscilloscope trace
mcqs.explain: The stronger stimulus produced four times as many impulses in the same time (200 per second rather than 50 per second) but no change in the height of the spikes. Action potentials are all-or-nothing, so stimulus strength is conveyed by how often they occur.
rationales: A student who reads spike height as stimulus strength picks this. In fact the peak of an action potential is fixed by the ion gradients and channels; the traces are exactly what is expected.
A student who thinks stimulus strength affects conduction speed picks this. In fact speed is a property of the fibre; the strong stimulus made the neuron fire more often, not faster.
A student who takes the spike count as the frequency picks this. In fact the traces cover only 100 ms, so the frequencies are 50 and 200 impulses per second.

The stronger stimulus produced four times as many impulses in the same time (200 per second rather than 50 per second) but no change in the height of the spikes. Action potentials are all-or-nothing, so stimulus strength is conveyed by how often they occur.

mcqs.q: Which statement explains saltatory conduction in a myelinated nerve fibre?
options: Ion channels and pumps are clustered at the nodes of Ranvier, so action potentials occur only at the nodes and the impulse passes from node to node.
The myelin sheath conducts the electrical current along the fibre, so the impulse travels through the myelin between the nodes.
Action potentials occur along the entire membrane of the fibre, but the myelin makes each of them develop more quickly.
The nodes of Ranvier are gaps in the insulation where the impulse leaks out, so each node slows the impulse slightly.
mcqs.specStatementText: Myelin lets the impulse jump from node to node
mcqs.explain: Myelin insulates the fibre between nodes, and the ion pumps and voltage-gated channels are clustered at the nodes of Ranvier. Local currents spread along the insulated section to the next node, which is depolarized to threshold, so the action potential is propagated from node to node.
rationales: Myelin insulates the fibre between nodes, and the ion pumps and voltage-gated channels are clustered at the nodes of Ranvier. Local currents spread along the insulated section to the next node, which is depolarized to threshold, so the action potential is propagated from node to node.

A student who thinks myelin is a conductor picks this. In fact myelin is an insulator that prevents ion movement across the covered membrane; the current flows inside and outside the axon, not through the myelin.
A student who keeps the non-myelinated mechanism picks this. In fact the myelinated sections lack the clustered channels and do not produce action potentials; only the nodes do.
A student who sees the nodes as faults in the insulation picks this. In fact the nodes are where the action potential is regenerated, and jumping between them is what makes conduction fast.

mcqs.q: Why does a myelinated fibre conduct impulses faster than a non-myelinated fibre of the same diameter?
options: Myelin is a good conductor of electricity, so the current flows through it faster than it can flow through the cytoplasm of the axon.
Depolarization has to occur only at the nodes, so far fewer regions of membrane are depolarized along the length of the fibre.
A myelinated fibre has fewer nodes than a non-myelinated one, and it is the nodes that slow the impulse down.
Action potentials form all along the fibre, but each one is generated more quickly beneath the insulating myelin.
mcqs.specStatementText: Myelin lets the impulse jump from node to node
mcqs.explain: In a non-myelinated fibre every region of membrane must be brought to threshold in turn. In a myelinated fibre the action potential is propagated from node to node, so only the nodes are depolarized and the impulse covers the same distance in far fewer steps.
rationales: A student who thinks myelin conducts picks this. In fact myelin insulates; the speed comes from restricting action potentials to the nodes.

In a non-myelinated fibre every region of membrane must be brought to threshold in turn. In a myelinated fibre the action potential is propagated from node to node, so only the nodes are depolarized and the impulse covers the same distance in far fewer steps.
A student who sees nodes as obstacles picks this. In fact a non-myelinated fibre has no nodes at all, and the nodes are where the action potential is regenerated, not where it is slowed.
A student who assumes myelin just speeds each action potential picks this. In fact no action potentials occur beneath the myelin; they occur only at the nodes.

mcqs.q: Cocaine binds to the transporter proteins that return dopamine to the presynaptic neuron. What effect does this have at a dopamine synapse?
options: Dopamine cannot bind to its postsynaptic receptors because they are blocked, so the postsynaptic neuron receives less stimulation than normal.
Transmission is inhibited, because any drug that acts at a synapse prevents the postsynaptic neuron from firing.
Dopamine remains in the synaptic cleft and continues to bind to postsynaptic receptors, so the postsynaptic neuron is stimulated for longer.
Dopamine release stops, because dopamine can only leave the presynaptic neuron through the transporter proteins that cocaine has blocked.
mcqs.specStatementText: Chemicals from outside can block or prolong transmission
mcqs.explain: Cocaine blocks reuptake of the neurotransmitter. Dopamine that would normally be removed from the cleft by the transporter proteins stays there, repeatedly binding to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane and prolonging its stimulation.
rationales: A student who assumes 'blocks' means blocking the receptor picks this. In fact cocaine blocks the transporter, not the receptor, so dopamine binds to the receptors more, not less.
A student who thinks all synaptic drugs are inhibitory picks this. In fact blocking reuptake increases stimulation of the postsynaptic neuron.

Cocaine blocks reuptake of the neurotransmitter. Dopamine that would normally be removed from the cleft by the transporter proteins stays there, repeatedly binding to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane and prolonging its stimulation.

A student who thinks neurotransmitter leaves by diffusing through membrane proteins rather than by exocytosis picks this. In fact dopamine is released from vesicles by exocytosis; the transporters only carry it back in, so release continues and dopamine accumulates in the cleft.

mcqs.q: How do neonicotinoid pesticides block synaptic transmission in insects?
options: They block the reuptake of acetylcholine into the presynaptic neuron, so the insect's synapses soon run out of neurotransmitter.
They inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase in the cleft, so acetylcholine is not broken down at all after it has been released.
They prevent calcium ions from crossing the synaptic cleft, so the postsynaptic membrane is not depolarized at all.
They bind to acetylcholine receptors at the insect's synapses, so acetylcholine can no longer transmit signals across them.
mcqs.specStatementText: Chemicals from outside can block or prolong transmission
mcqs.explain: Neonicotinoids bind to acetylcholine receptors on postsynaptic membranes in the insect's central nervous system. The receptors can then no longer respond normally to acetylcholine, so synaptic transmission is blocked and the insect is paralysed and dies.
rationales: A student who has merged the two examples picks this. In fact blocking reuptake is the mechanism of cocaine; neonicotinoids act at the acetylcholine receptors.
A student who expects a pesticide to target the enzyme picks this. In fact that is the action of other insecticides; neonicotinoids bind to the receptors, not the enzyme.
A student who thinks calcium crosses the cleft picks this. In fact calcium acts inside the presynaptic neuron, and neonicotinoids act on the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors.

Neonicotinoids bind to acetylcholine receptors on postsynaptic membranes in the insect's central nervous system. The receptors can then no longer respond normally to acetylcholine, so synaptic transmission is blocked and the insect is paralysed and dies.

mcqs.q: What happens at the postsynaptic membrane when an inhibitory neurotransmitter binds to its receptors?
options: Channels open that make the inside more negative than the resting potential, so the membrane is hyperpolarized and further from threshold.
Channels open that depolarize the membrane, but by a smaller amount than an excitatory neurotransmitter would.
Channels open that make the inside more positive than the resting potential, which is called hyperpolarization.
Nothing happens at this membrane, because inhibitory neurotransmitters act by stopping release from the presynaptic neuron.
mcqs.specStatementText: Inhibitory neurotransmitters make the inside more negative
mcqs.explain: Inhibitory neurotransmitters open channels that let negative ions such as chloride ions in or positive ions such as potassium ions out. The postsynaptic membrane becomes hyperpolarized, generating an inhibitory postsynaptic potential that makes an action potential less likely.
rationales: Inhibitory neurotransmitters open channels that let negative ions such as chloride ions in or positive ions such as potassium ions out. The postsynaptic membrane becomes hyperpolarized, generating an inhibitory postsynaptic potential that makes an action potential less likely.
A student who thinks 'inhibitory' just means 'weaker' picks this. In fact inhibitory neurotransmitters move the membrane potential the opposite way, making it more negative.
A student who reads 'hyper' as 'more positive' picks this. In fact hyperpolarization means more polarized: more negative inside than at rest.
A student who thinks inhibition switches off the presynaptic neuron picks this. In fact the inhibitory neurotransmitter is itself released and acts on the postsynaptic membrane, hyperpolarizing it.

mcqs.q: A postsynaptic neuron has a resting potential of −70 mV and a threshold of −55 mV. At the same moment it receives two excitatory inputs, each producing a +8 mV change, and one inhibitory input producing a −6 mV change. What is the result?
options: An action potential, because the two excitatory inputs alone take the membrane to −54 mV.
No action potential, because the combined change takes the membrane only to −60 mV.
Two action potentials, one triggered by each of the two excitatory inputs that arrive.
A small action potential of 10 mV, matching the net change in the membrane potential.
mcqs.specStatementText: Inputs add up, and the outcome is all or nothing
mcqs.explain: Summation adds the postsynaptic potentials: −70 + 8 + 8 − 6 = −60 mV. This does not reach the threshold of −55 mV, so the all-or-nothing consequence is that no action potential is produced.
rationales: A student who thinks inhibitory inputs cannot cancel excitatory ones ignores the −6 mV. In fact all inputs are summed, and the inhibitory hyperpolarization keeps the membrane at −60 mV, below threshold.
Summation adds the postsynaptic potentials: −70 + 8 + 8 − 6 = −60 mV. This does not reach the threshold of −55 mV, so the all-or-nothing consequence is that no action potential is produced.
A student who thinks every excitatory input fires the neuron picks this. In fact a single +8 mV input is far below threshold, and inputs are summed rather than counted.
A student who thinks action potentials are graded picks this. In fact action potentials are all-or-nothing; a net depolarization below threshold produces none.

mcqs.q: Which statement about summation at a postsynaptic neuron is correct?
options: Each impulse arriving from any presynaptic neuron produces its own action potential in the postsynaptic neuron.
Postsynaptic potentials are all-or-nothing, so each one is either a full-sized action potential or nothing at all.
Postsynaptic potentials from several presynaptic neurons add together, and an action potential results only if threshold is reached.
Inhibitory and excitatory inputs act on separate parts of the membrane and so cannot cancel each other out.
mcqs.specStatementText: Inputs add up, and the outcome is all or nothing
mcqs.explain: Multiple presynaptic neurons interact at a postsynaptic neuron. Their excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials are summed, and the consequence is all-or-nothing: an action potential is produced if the net depolarization reaches threshold and not otherwise.
rationales: A student who pictures a synapse as a one-to-one relay picks this. In fact a single input is usually too small to reach threshold, which is why summation is needed.
A student who confuses postsynaptic potentials with action potentials picks this. In fact postsynaptic potentials are graded and add together; only the action potential is all-or-nothing.

Multiple presynaptic neurons interact at a postsynaptic neuron. Their excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials are summed, and the consequence is all-or-nothing: an action potential is produced if the net depolarization reaches threshold and not otherwise.
A student who treats excitation and inhibition as independent switches picks this. In fact both change the same membrane potential in opposite directions, so they do cancel.

mcqs.q: Eating chilli peppers causes a burning pain in the mouth. Which explanation is correct?
options: Capsaicin raises the temperature of the tissue in the mouth, and this heat is what the free nerve endings then detect.
Capsaicin stimulates free nerve endings, which perceive the pain in the mouth and then send a report of it to the brain.
Capsaicin causes receptor cells in the mouth to release neurotransmitter onto sensory neurons, which then carry the pain.
Capsaicin opens channels for positive ions in free nerve endings, so threshold is reached and impulses pass to the brain, where pain is perceived.
mcqs.specStatementText: Free nerve endings detect painful stimuli; the brain feels pain
mcqs.explain: Free nerve endings have channels for positively charged ions that open in response to high temperature, acid, or chemicals such as capsaicin. Entry of positive ions brings the membrane to threshold, and the impulses that result pass to the brain, where the pain is perceived.
rationales: A student who takes 'hot' literally picks this. In fact the tissue does not warm; capsaicin opens the same channels that heat opens, so the brain perceives the same burning.
A student who locates perception at the site of the stimulus picks this. In fact the nerve endings only detect the stimulus and generate impulses; pain is perceived in the brain.
A student who expects separate receptor cells picks this. In fact the free nerve endings are part of the sensory neurons themselves, and capsaicin acts directly on their ion channels.

Free nerve endings have channels for positively charged ions that open in response to high temperature, acid, or chemicals such as capsaicin. Entry of positive ions brings the membrane to threshold, and the impulses that result pass to the brain, where the pain is perceived.

mcqs.q: A local anaesthetic blocks the voltage-gated sodium channels in the sensory neurons of a patch of skin. A hot object is then placed on the skin, but no pain is felt. Why?
options: Positive ions still enter the free nerve endings, but no impulses can be propagated to the brain, where pain is perceived.
The channels that respond to heat are voltage-gated, so they are blocked too and no positive ions can enter.
The skin is where pain is perceived, and the anaesthetic has stopped the skin from perceiving the heat.
The anaesthetic cools the skin, so the free nerve endings are not exposed to a temperature high enough to respond.
mcqs.specStatementText: Free nerve endings detect painful stimuli; the brain feels pain
mcqs.explain: The heat-sensitive channels in the free nerve endings are opened by the stimulus, not by voltage, so positive ions still enter and threshold may be reached. Without voltage-gated sodium channels, however, no action potentials can be generated or propagated, so nothing reaches the brain and no pain is perceived.
rationales: The heat-sensitive channels in the free nerve endings are opened by the stimulus, not by voltage, so positive ions still enter and threshold may be reached. Without voltage-gated sodium channels, however, no action potentials can be generated or propagated, so nothing reaches the brain and no pain is perceived.
A student who thinks every channel in a neuron is voltage-gated picks this. In fact the stimulus-sensitive channels open in response to heat itself; it is the later impulse that is prevented.
A student who locates perception in the skin picks this. In fact the skin's nerve endings detect; pain is perceived in the brain, which the impulses cannot now reach.
A student who thinks pain-related chemicals act by changing temperature picks this. In fact the anaesthetic acts on ion channels, not on temperature, and the hot object still heats the skin.

mcqs.q: Why is consciousness described as an emergent property of the brain?
options: It is stored in a particular small group of neurons in the brain that are specialized for consciousness.
It arises from the interaction of very many neurons and is not a property of any individual neuron.
Each neuron in the brain contributes a small amount of consciousness, and these amounts add up to the whole.
It is produced by a single neurotransmitter, which is released throughout the brain whenever a person is awake.
mcqs.specStatementText: Consciousness emerges from neurons interacting
mcqs.explain: Emergent properties are consequences of interaction. Consciousness emerges from the interaction of individual neurons in the brain; no single neuron is conscious, and the property cannot be found by studying neurons one at a time.
rationales: A student who expects consciousness to have a location picks this. In fact it is not stored anywhere; it emerges from interactions across very many neurons.

Emergent properties are consequences of interaction. Consciousness emerges from the interaction of individual neurons in the brain; no single neuron is conscious, and the property cannot be found by studying neurons one at a time.
A student who thinks emergent means additive picks this. In fact no neuron is conscious to any degree; the property appears only from the interactions.
A student who links mental states to single chemicals picks this. In fact consciousness cannot be reduced to one molecule; it emerges from the interaction of neurons.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic C2.2 Neural signalling

specStatements.text: A neuron is one cell with a body and long fibres
Pumping ions sets up the resting potential
A nerve impulse is a travelling reversal of membrane potential
Wider and myelinated fibres conduct faster
Synapses join neurons to neurons or to effectors, one way only
Neurotransmitter opens channels and depolarizes the postsynaptic cell
Voltage-gated channels drive depolarization and repolarization
Local currents carry the action potential along
Myelin lets the impulse jump from node to node
Chemicals from outside can block or prolong transmission
Inhibitory neurotransmitters make the inside more negative
Inputs add up, and the outcome is all or nothing
Free nerve endings detect painful stimuli; the brain feels pain

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every synapse in this bank is a chemical synapse and is called simply a synapse. Electrical synapses, gap junctions and connexons are not mentioned anywhere in the concepts, misconceptions or items, and no item asks students to distinguish the two types.

omitted.sequence: no authored ordering; would require inventing a sequence
